title: Hidden Costs of Building a House: Permits, Utilities, Neighbours, Fit-Out
desc: Costs few people budget for when building: procedures, site utilities, compensating adjacent houses, screening, insurance, furnishings. A checklist for owners.
summary: A list of hidden costs of building a house that contractors' quotations usually omit, helping owners budget sufficiently and avoid being caught off guard.
body: A construction quotation usually covers only the building and finishing work. Once work starts, owners run into a series of costs that “nobody mentioned”. Listing them in advance makes the budget more realistic.

Design drawings: a house of 3 floors or more, with a basement, with total floor area of 250 m² or more, or 12 m or higher must be designed by a qualified person (Clause 2, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP).
Construction permit (if required): application documents, drawings, fees (if any) – see Procedure for applying for a construction permit for a private house.

As-built completion (hoàn công) and registering the house on the land use right certificate: surveying, extracts. Good news: a self-built house of a household or individual is exempt from the registration fee (Clause 11, Article 10 of Consolidated Document 33/VBHN-BTC).
2. Electricity, water and the work site

Temporary electricity and water meters for the site; electricity and water charges throughout construction; demolishing the old house, hauling away debris, levelling the ground. When preparing an estimate for a state project, construction costs include temporary housing for living and for managing the works (Point đ, Clause 2, Article 12 of Decree 206/2026/ND-CP) – for private houses, ask whether the quotation already includes these items.
When building you must ensure safety and not infringe the lawful rights and interests of owners of adjacent and surrounding houses (Article 174 of the Civil Code).
If a house or building causes damage to others, its owner must pay compensation; if the builder is at fault, they are jointly liable (Article 605).

It is advisable to photograph and record the condition of the neighbouring house before excavating foundations, and to budget for shoring and repairs if cracks or dampness appear. See Building causes a neighbour's house to settle or crack: who pays?

Screening nets, scaffolding, site signs, debris collection, washing vehicles leaving the site. The owner must install a construction site sign at the entrance (Point a, Clause 3, Article 10). Failing to screen or allowing spillage can be fined – see Fines for safety and screening violations during construction.

The Construction Law 2025 lists insurance for workers on the site and third-party civil liability insurance purchased by the construction contractor as compulsory insurance; the Government prescribes the detailed conditions and premium rates (Clauses 1 and 3, Article 10). Ask the contractor whether the quotation already includes insurance and who bears the cost; the parties agree on responsibility for buying insurance in the contract (Clause 1, Article 20 of Decree 210/2026/ND-CP).
Loose furniture: beds, wardrobes, sofas, curtains, decorative lights.
Appliances: air conditioners, water heaters, water purifiers, kitchen, cameras, internet.
Gate, yard, plants, canopies, protective grilles (if outside the contract).

Before signing the contract, mark each item above as “already in the quotation”, “family arranges it” or “not yet counted”. Add each “not yet counted” item to the budget or contingency fund. If you need help reviewing the quotation and budget, you can contact Quan Construction.

This article is for reference only and is not financial or legal advice. Construction permit fees, surveying costs and local charges are not in our library; ask the commune or ward People's Committee where you are building. The decree giving detailed rules on compulsory insurance in construction activities is not yet in our library.
